profile.campus: Red Oak, Ellis County, Texas (Google's second Texas data center campus, announced 2023, first building operational late 2025)
profile.address: North State Highway 342, Red Oak, Ellis County, Texas, 75154
profile.reading:
This building is part of Google's Red Oak, Texas data center campus, the company's second in Ellis County after its original Midlothian site. Google announced the Red Oak project in 2023, planning to invest more than $600 million overall including an initial $330 million in its first year in Texas, at a site the company itself has given as 156 N. Austin Boulevard in Red Oak spanning roughly 285,000 square feet; construction was expected to take about two years. Google said the completed facility would support 30 permanent full-time positions, while construction generated nearly 1,200 temporary jobs, and framed the project as supporting growing demand for its cloud, Workspace, and Maps services. The Ellis County Press reported the Red Oak campus's first building became operational by late 2025, and on September 2, 2026, Google folded continued Red Oak buildout into a broader $40 billion Texas investment announcement through 2027 that also includes a fourth building at the nearby Midlothian campus, part of what Google has described as three AI-focused data center hubs across the state. This particular OSM-mapped building sits on North State Highway 342 rather than the N. Austin Boulevard address Google has given for the campus overall, likely reflecting a different building or access point on the same Red Oak site; Google's own Ellis County location page does not break out individual building addresses or MW capacity, consistent with its general disclosure practice.

Ercot, the grid operator for most of Texas, has flagged data center and large-load interconnection requests, heavily concentrated in North Texas corridors like Ellis County, as a major driver behind its 2026 long-term load forecasts, prompting new large-load interconnection study procedures the Public Utility Commission of Texas adopted to manage how quickly hyperscale campuses like Google's Midlothian and Red Oak sites can add capacity to the grid. Ellis County's own economic development materials have cited the Red Oak and Midlothian projects together as the county's largest capital investment in its history, ahead of any prior manufacturing or logistics project the county had previously recruited.

reading.body:
Google operates a data center campus in Ellis County, Texas near Red Oak as part of a broader Midlothian complex where it has filed for a fifth building within a three-AI-data-center expansion announced across Texas. Google does not publish exact power capacity for individual facilities, only aggregate state-level investment figures on its own data center pages. A third-party aggregator reports roughly 86 MW for the Midlothian campus, but this figure is not confirmed by Google and should be treated as an unverified estimate.

If the 86 MW aggregator figure is accurate, this would represent a single large training or inference campus. At typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, 86 MW of IT load would support roughly 2,100 racks. The campus would rank below the 18 facilities in Texas with published power specifications, though 133 facilities are mapped in the state and most publish no figures.

Google's disclosure policy makes this campus invisible to capacity tracking. Texas published capacity totals 468 MW across 18 disclosed facilities, but Google's actual footprint in the state is unknown. The Midlothian campus matters to AI scaling primarily as an example of how large deployments by major operators remain opaque to the public record, leaving grid planners and capacity researchers unable to verify whether announced expansions are actually built.
